restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions in the effervescent tablet or oral solution SmPCs. SPS notes modified-release potassium tablets are considered less suitable for NHS prescribing.

items.t: Adults and children: usually 2 to 4 tablets daily (24 to 48 mmol K+) for prophylaxis or treatment; adjust to diet, clinical state and serum electrolytes.

src.q: the administration of 2 to 4 tablets daily (24 to 48 mmol K+) is likely to provide an adequate prophylactic or therapeutic dose in most patients

items.t: More severe depletion: serum K+ 2-3 mmol/l, consider up to 100-200 mmol K+ per day (8-16 tablets); serum K+ 3-4 mmol/l, consider up to 50-100 mmol K+ per day (4-8 tablets). Serum K+ below 2 mmol/l may need IV replacement.
items.tag: Effervescent tablets: maximum daily doses by serum potassium

src.q: For serum levels between 2-3 mmol/l, a maximum daily dose of 100-200 mmol K+ (8-16 tablets)
for serum levels between 3-4 mmol/l, a maximum daily dose of 50-100 mmol K+ (4-8 tablets) should be considered
serum potassium levels below 2 mmol/l may warrant intravenous replacement therapy

items.t: Adults: 10 to 50 mL (10 to 50 mmol K+) per day in divided amounts after food; adjust to cause, degree and duration of depletion.

src.q: Adults: 10 - 50 mL/day in divided amounts after food is usually an adequate dosage.
equivalent to 1 millimole of potassium per ml

items.t: Elderly: usually no special adjustment, but take renal insufficiency into account; monitor serum potassium if clinically needed (oral solution SmPC). Supervise carefully (effervescent tablet SmPC).

src.q: concurrent renal insufficiency should be taken into account
such patients should be carefully supervised

items.t: SPS (adults, acute): mild hypokalaemia (3.0-3.5 mmol/L) oral 24 mmol potassium up to 2 to 3 times a day; moderate (2.5-2.9 mmol/L) oral 24 to 36 mmol up to 3 to 4 times a day. Severe (below 2.5 mmol/L): IV potassium in hospital.

src.q: Up to 1 year: The usual dose is 0.5 - 0.75 mL/kg body weight/day in divided amounts after food.
Aged 1 to 12 years: The usual dose is 0.5 - 1.0 mL/kg body weight/day in divided amounts after food.
The dose should be administered using a graduated dropper.

src.q: This is particularly important in patients with cardiac disease and in those receiving digitalis.

items.t: Oral solution SmPC: caution with a history of peptic ulcer. Potassium chloride can cause GI ulceration, haemorrhage or stricture (lower oesophagus, small bowel), more likely with local GI disorders, cardiovascular disease or prolonged therapy.

src.q: Oral potassium should be prescribed with caution in patients with a history of peptic ulcer.
may induce ulceration, haemorrhage or stricture formation in the gastrointestinal tract, in particular the lower oesophagus and the small bowel

items.t: Acidosis: monitor acid-base balance. Hypertension: correcting hypokalaemia may lower blood pressure.

items.t: Excipients: the effervescent tablets (sucrose) and the oral solution (sorbitol) should not be taken in hereditary fructose intolerance; the oral solution contains E122 and parabens (may cause allergic reactions).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: ACE inhibitors (e.g. lisinopril): risk of hyperkalaemia; use with caution. Lisinopril SmPC: combination with potassium supplements is not recommended; if needed, use with caution and frequent serum potassium monitoring.

src.q: If co-administered with potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE-inhibitors, the risk of hyperkalaemia must be considered.
Therefore, the combination of Lisinopril tablet with the above-mentioned drugs is not recommended.
If concomitant use is indicated, they should be used with caution and with frequent monitoring of serum potassium.

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics and aldosterone antagonists (e.g. spironolactone): risk of hyperkalaemia. Spironolactone SmPC: potassium supplements should not be given routinely with spironolactone.
